item.title: AI Architect Interview Path
item.description: Two weeks at one to two hours a day covers the whole path. If you have less time, read the two case studies and the interview section first, then fill gaps from the linked articles.

item.title: How to Answer AI System Design Interviews
item.description:
Why a framework#

AI system design interviews test whether you can turn a vague product idea into an architecture that is useful, safe, measurable and affordable. Without a structure, candidates jump to “use a vector DB and GPT” and miss requirements, evaluation and risk — the parts interviewers weigh most for senior and architect roles.

item.title: How Large Language Models Work
item.description:
Simple definition#

A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained to predict the next piece of text. Given “The capital of France is”, it assigns a probability to every possible next token and “Paris” scores highest. Repeating that prediction one token at a time produces sentences, code, plans and answers.

item.title: RAG Fundamentals: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
item.description:
Simple definition#

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) answers a question in two steps: first retrieve the most relevant pieces of your own documents, then ask the LLM to generate an answer using those pieces as context.

Analogy: an open-book exam. The model is a smart student who has not read your company handbook. RAG hands them the right pages before they answer.

item.title: Spring AI Fundamentals
item.description:
Simple definition#

Spring AI is the Spring project for building AI applications in Java. It gives you portable APIs for chat, embeddings, images, audio and vector stores across many providers, plus higher-level building blocks — a fluent ChatClient, advisors for RAG and memory, tool calling, MCP, structured output and observability — all configured the Spring Boot way.

item.title: What Is an AI Agent?
item.description:
Simple definition#

An AI agent is a system where an LLM decides what to do next, does it by calling tools, observes the result, and repeats until the goal is reached or it must stop.

A chatbot answers. An agent acts: it can look up an order, check a policy, issue a refund, and email the customer — choosing the steps itself.

item.title: Chunking and Embeddings
item.description:
Simple definition#

  • Chunking is splitting documents into smaller passages so that search can return just the relevant part, and so it fits in the prompt.
  • An embedding is a list of numbers (a vector) that represents the meaning of a piece of text. Texts with similar meaning have vectors that are close together.

Together they decide what your RAG system can find.

item.title: LLM Inference, Latency and Cost
item.description:
Simple definition#

Inference is running a trained model to produce output. For an LLM it has two phases: reading the whole prompt (prefill) and then generating the answer one token at a time (decode). Almost every latency, throughput and cost decision in an AI system traces back to these two phases.

item.title: Interview Question Bank: Enterprise and Agentic AI
item.description:
Answers are deliberately short — the length you would say aloud before the interviewer follows up. Each section links to the article with the full explanation.

item.title: RAG with Spring AI
item.description:
What we are building#

A Spring Boot service that ingests policy documents into PostgreSQL with pgvector, then answers questions with citations, filtered by the user’s department.

Dependencies and configuration#

<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.ai</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-ai-starter-vector-store-pgvector</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.ai</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-ai-vector-store-advisor</artifactId>    <!-- QuestionAnswerAdvisor -->
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.ai</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-ai-rag</artifactId>                     <!-- RetrievalAugmentationAdvisor -->
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.ai</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-ai-pdf-document-reader</artifactId>
</dependency>
<!-- plus a chat model starter and an embedding model starter, e.g. OpenAI or Bedrock -->

spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/assistant
spring.ai.vectorstore.pgvector.initialize-schema=true
spring.ai.vectorstore.pgvector.index-type=HNSW
spring.ai.vectorstore.pgvector.distance-type=COSINE_DISTANCE
spring.ai.vectorstore.pgvector.dimensions=1536

The starter auto-configures a VectorStore bean using the EmbeddingModel bean from your embedding starter. In production, prefer creating the schema with your migration tool (Flyway/Liquibase) and set initialize-schema=false.

item.title: Tool Calling (Function Calling)
item.description:
Simple definition#

Tool calling (also called function calling) lets an LLM ask your application to run a function. You describe the available tools; the model replies with “call get_order with {"orderId": "8812"}”; your code runs it and sends the result back; the model continues.

item.title: Enterprise AI Cheat Sheet
item.description:
Numbers to know#

Item Rule of thumb
Token ↔ text 1 token ≈ 4 characters ≈ 0.75 English words; 1,000 tokens ≈ 750 words ≈ 1.5 pages
Output vs input price Output tokens typically cost 3–5× input tokens
Prompt caching Cached input often ~90% cheaper; needs a stable prefix
Batch APIs ~50% cheaper; results within hours
Generation speed Tens to a few hundred tokens/s depending on model and load
Total latency ≈ TTFT + output tokens ÷ tokens per second
Context windows ~128K to 1M+ tokens on current frontier models
Weights memory Parameters × bytes per parameter (FP16 = 2, INT8 = 1, INT4 = 0.5); 70B FP16 ≈ 140 GB
Vector storage vectors × dimensions × 4 bytes (float32); +~50% for HNSW graph
Chunk size 300–800 tokens, 10–20% overlap, plus heading context
Retrieval Retrieve 20–100 candidates → rerank → send 3–8
Golden dataset Start with 50–100 cases, grow to several hundred
Error compounding 0.95 per step over 10 steps ≈ 60% success

Cost formula#

monthly cost = requests/month × (input tokens × input price + output tokens × output price)
peak TPM     = peak requests/min × (input + output tokens per request)

Prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning#

Need Use
Task definition, format, tone Prompting (+ few-shot)
Private, fresh, citable, permissioned knowledge RAG
Consistent behaviour, domain style, cheaper small model Fine-tuning (LoRA)
Actions and live data Tools / agents

RAG pipeline at a glance#

Top upgrades by impact: parsing & structure-aware chunking → hybrid search → reranking → metadata/ACL filters → query rewriting → contextual retrieval → agentic/graph retrieval.

item.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
item.description:
Simple definition#

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data. An MCP server exposes capabilities — tools to call, resources to read, prompt templates to use — and any MCP-compatible AI application can discover and use them.

item.title: Prompt and Context Engineering
item.description:
Simple definition#

Prompt engineering is writing the instructions and examples that steer an LLM toward the output you need. Context engineering is the broader discipline of deciding everything that goes into the context window on each call — instructions, retrieved documents, memory, tool results — and in what order.

item.title: Agents with Spring AI: Tools, MCP and Memory
item.description:
What this article covers#

How the agent concepts from Module 3 map to Spring AI 2.0 code:

Concept Spring AI
Tool @Tool method, ToolCallback
Identity passed to tools ToolContext
Agent loop Built-in tool execution in ChatClient, or ToolCallingAdvisor
MCP client spring-ai-starter-mcp-client → tools as ToolCallbackProvider
MCP server spring-ai-starter-mcp-server-webmvc + @McpTool
Short-term memory ChatMemory + MessageChatMemoryAdvisor
Persistent memory JdbcChatMemoryRepository (and Redis, Cassandra, Mongo, Neo4j)

Tools with @Tool#

@Component
class OrderTools {

    private final OrderService orders;

    OrderTools(OrderService orders) { this.orders = orders; }

    @Tool(description = """
        Get status, items and delivery estimate of one of the current customer's orders.
        Use when the customer asks where an order is. Order numbers look like A-12345.""")
    OrderView getOrder(@ToolParam(description = "Order number, e.g. A-12345") String orderId,
                       ToolContext ctx) {
        String customerId = (String) ctx.getContext().get("customerId"); // from session, not the model
        return orders.findForCustomer(orderId, customerId)
                     .orElseThrow(() -> new ToolException("Order not found for this customer"));
    }

    @Tool(description = "Refund an order of the current customer. Amount in EUR.")
    RefundResult refund(String orderId, BigDecimal amount, String reason, ToolContext ctx) {
        String customerId = (String) ctx.getContext().get("customerId");
        return orders.requestRefund(orderId, customerId, amount, reason); // limits enforced here
    }
}

String reply = chatClient.prompt()
    .user(customerMessage)
    .tools(orderTools)
    .toolContext(Map.of("customerId", authenticatedCustomerId))
    .call()
    .content();
  • Spring AI generates JSON Schemas from method signatures; @ToolParam adds descriptions and required flags.
  • ToolContext passes data to the tool without sending it to the model — use it for identity, tenant and correlation IDs.
  • returnDirect = true on @Tool returns the result to the caller without another model round trip.
  • Exceptions can be converted into messages for the model so it can recover; keep them short and helpful. (ToolException above stands for your own exception type.)
  • Enforce business limits in OrderService, not in the prompt.

The tool-calling loop#

By default the tool loop runs inside the model call. In Spring AI 2.0 you can instead add ToolCallingAdvisor, which runs the loop inside the advisor chain, so other advisors (logging, memory, guardrails, auditing) see every iteration — useful for agent observability and per-step policy checks.

item.title: Vector Databases Explained
item.description:
Simple definition#

A vector database stores embeddings (vectors) together with their text and metadata, and answers one question fast: “which stored vectors are closest to this query vector?” — usually with filters such as “only documents this user may see”.

item.title: Advanced RAG: Hybrid Search, Reranking, Query Transformation and Agentic RAG
item.description:
Simple definition#

Advanced RAG adds steps before, during and after retrieval to find better context: fix the question (pre-retrieval), search in more than one way (retrieval), and filter and order what was found (post-retrieval). Agentic RAG goes further and lets an LLM decide when, where and how many times to search.

item.title: Prompting vs RAG vs Fine-Tuning
item.description:
Simple definition#

There are three main ways to make a general-purpose LLM useful for your business:

  • Prompting — change the instructions the model receives.
  • RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) — change the knowledge the model receives, by retrieving relevant documents into the prompt.
  • Fine-tuning — change the model’s weights by training it further on your examples.

A useful slogan: RAG for knowledge, fine-tuning for behaviour, prompting for everything first.

item.title: Spring AI in Production
item.description:
What changes in production#

A demo calls a model and prints the answer. A production service must be observable (what did it do, how long, at what cost), tested (evaluated on a dataset), resilient (timeouts, retries, fallbacks), secure and governed. Spring AI plugs into the Spring Boot production toolkit you already use for this.

item.title: Agentic Workflow Patterns
item.description:
Simple definition#

Agentic patterns are reusable shapes for combining LLM calls, tools and code — the “design patterns” of AI systems. Most production systems are a composition of a few of them. They range from fully code-controlled workflows to fully model-controlled agents.

item.title: AI Security: OWASP LLM Top 10, Prompt Injection and Agent Security
item.description:
Simple definition#

AI security protects AI systems — models, prompts, data, tools and agents — from being manipulated, leaking information, or being used to cause harm. Classic application security still applies; LLMs add a new problem: instructions and data travel in the same channel (natural language), so data can act like code.

item.title: GraphRAG and Knowledge Graphs
item.description:
Simple definition#

A knowledge graph stores facts as entities (nodes: people, products, systems, contracts) and relationships (edges: owns, depends on, supplies). GraphRAG uses such a graph — often built automatically from documents by an LLM — to retrieve connected facts and summaries that plain vector search cannot find.

item.title: Model Selection for the Enterprise
item.description:
Simple definition#

Model selection is choosing which LLM (or which mix of LLMs) serves each use case, based on quality for the task, cost, latency, data-protection requirements and operational fit. In an enterprise it is not a one-time choice: models change every few months, so the architecture must make swapping cheap.

item.title: Multi-Agent Systems
item.description:
Simple definition#

A multi-agent system splits work among several agents, each with its own instructions, tools and context, which coordinate to reach a goal. It is the AI equivalent of a team: a lead delegates to specialists.

item.title: AI Governance and Responsible AI
item.description:
Simple definition#

AI governance is the set of policies, roles, processes and technical controls that make sure an organisation’s AI is lawful, safe, fair, secure, transparent and accountable — and that someone is answerable for each system. Responsible AI names the principles; governance is how you put them into practice.

item.title: The Enterprise AI Stack: Reference Architecture
item.description:
Simple definition#

The enterprise AI stack is the set of shared layers an organisation builds so that many teams can ship AI features safely and cheaply: access to models, a gateway to control that access, pipelines that turn company data into retrievable knowledge, frameworks for chains and agents, and the operations, security and governance around all of it.

item.title: Agent Memory, State and Durable Execution
item.description:
Simple definition#

LLMs are stateless: each call knows only what is in its prompt. Memory is everything your system stores and feeds back so an agent can continue a conversation, remember a user’s preferences, learn from past cases, and resume a long task after a crash.

item.title: Evaluating RAG and LLM Applications
item.description:
Simple definition#

Evaluation is measuring how well your AI system does its job, on a fixed set of test cases, with repeatable scores. For RAG you measure two things separately: did we find the right information (retrieval), and did we use it correctly (generation)?

item.title: System Design: Enterprise Knowledge Assistant (RAG)
item.description:
The interview question#

“Design an AI assistant that lets 50,000 employees ask questions about internal policies, procedures and technical documentation, with answers grounded in company documents.”

This walk-through follows the AI system design framework.

1. Requirements#

Functional

item.title: LLMOps: Running AI in Production
item.description:
Simple definition#

LLMOps is the set of practices for building, deploying, monitoring and improving LLM applications in production. It extends DevOps and MLOps with things specific to LLMs: prompts as versioned artefacts, evaluation of non-deterministic output, token cost, safety guardrails and traces of multi-step chains and agents.

item.title: Agent Reliability, Guardrails and Evaluation
item.description:
Simple definition#

Agent reliability is the engineering that makes an agent do the right thing consistently, stop when it should, and fail safely when it cannot succeed. It combines guardrails (prevent bad actions), budgets (bound cost and time), evaluation (measure behaviour before and after release) and observability (see what happened).

item.title: About this handbook
item.description:
Purpose#

The Enterprise AI & Agentic AI Knowledge Hub explains strategic AI architecture simply, for architects and senior engineers who design, build or govern AI systems — and for anyone preparing for AI architecture interviews. It is the companion to the Java & Software Architecture Knowledge Hub.

item.title: Glossary
item.description:
Definitions are deliberately short. Follow the links for the full explanation.

A#

A2A (Agent2Agent protocol)
An open protocol for agents to discover each other through agent cards and delegate tasks. See Multi-agent systems.
Advisor (Spring AI)
An interceptor around a ChatClient call, used for memory, RAG, logging, tool loops and custom concerns. See Spring AI fundamentals.
Agent
An LLM-driven system that loops — reason, act through tools, observe — until a goal is met. See What is an agent?
Agentic RAG
RAG where an agent decides when and where to retrieve, possibly several times. See Advanced retrieval.
AI gateway
The single controlled entry point to all models: auth, quotas, guardrails, routing, caching, logging, cost. See Enterprise AI stack.
ANN (approximate nearest neighbour)
Search that finds most of the closest vectors quickly without comparing all of them. See Vector databases.
Attention
The transformer mechanism by which each token weighs and uses information from other tokens. See How LLMs work.

B–C#

BM25
A classic keyword relevance ranking function used in sparse/keyword search. See Advanced retrieval.
Chunking
Splitting documents into passages for retrieval. See Chunking and embeddings.
Context engineering
Deciding everything that goes into the context window on each call. See Prompt and context engineering.
Context window
The maximum tokens (input + output) a model processes per call. See How LLMs work.
Contextual retrieval
Prepending an LLM-written situating sentence to each chunk before indexing. See Advanced retrieval.
Cross-encoder / reranker
A model that scores a query and a document together for precise relevance. See Advanced retrieval.

D–E#

Distillation
Training a small model on a large model’s outputs. See Prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning.
Embedding
A vector representing the meaning of text. See Chunking and embeddings.
EU AI Act
The EU regulation classifying AI systems by risk tier with matching obligations. See AI governance.
Evaluator–optimizer
A loop where one LLM generates and another critiques until criteria are met. See Workflow patterns.
Excessive agency
An LLM system with more tools, permissions or autonomy than it needs. See AI security.

F–H#

Faithfulness (groundedness)
Whether every claim in an answer is supported by the retrieved context. See RAG evaluation.
Fine-tuning
Further training of a model’s weights on your examples. See Prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning.
Golden dataset
A versioned set of test cases with expected answers used for evaluation. See RAG evaluation.
GraphRAG
RAG over a knowledge graph of entities, relationships and community summaries. See GraphRAG.
Guardrails
Checks on inputs, actions and outputs that keep an AI system within policy. See Agent reliability.
Hallucination
Fluent but unsupported or false model output. See How LLMs work.
HNSW
A multi-layer graph index for fast approximate vector search. See Vector databases.
Human-in-the-loop (HITL)
Pausing an AI process for human approval, correction or input. See Workflow patterns.
Hybrid search
Combining vector and keyword search, usually fused with RRF. See Advanced retrieval.
HyDE
Searching with the embedding of an LLM-generated hypothetical answer. See Advanced retrieval.

K–L#

KV cache
Stored attention keys and values that speed up generation. See Inference.
Lethal trifecta
Private data + untrusted content + external communication in one agent. See AI security.
LLM-as-a-judge
Using an LLM with a rubric to grade outputs. See RAG evaluation.
LLMOps
Practices for operating LLM applications. See LLMOps.
LoRA
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning with small low-rank adapters. See Prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning.

M–N#

MCP (Model Context Protocol)
An open protocol for AI applications to use tools, resources and prompts from servers. See MCP.
Mixture of Experts (MoE)
A model architecture that routes each token to a few expert sub-networks. See How LLMs work.
Model routing
Sending each request to the cheapest capable model. See Model selection.
MRR / nDCG
Retrieval ranking metrics. See RAG evaluation.
NIST AI RMF
A risk-management framework with Govern, Map, Measure and Manage functions. See AI governance.

O–R#

Orchestrator–workers
A central LLM dynamically delegating sub-tasks to workers. See Workflow patterns.
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications
The ten most critical security risks for LLM apps. See AI security.
Prompt caching
Reusing computation for a repeated prompt prefix. See Inference.
Prompt injection
Input that makes a model follow attacker instructions. See AI security.
Quantization
Storing weights or vectors at lower precision to save memory. See Inference.
RAG (retrieval-augmented generation)
Retrieving relevant passages and generating an answer grounded in them. See RAG fundamentals.
ReAct
An agent pattern interleaving reasoning, actions and observations. See What is an agent?
Reasoning model
A model trained to think step by step before answering. See How LLMs work.
RRF (reciprocal rank fusion)
Merging ranked lists by summing 1/(k + rank). See Advanced retrieval.

S–Z#

Structured output
Model output constrained to a schema and parsed into types. See Prompt engineering.
Temperature
A sampling setting controlling randomness. See How LLMs work.
Token
The sub-word unit models read and write. See How LLMs work.
Tool calling (function calling)
The model requesting your application to run a function. See Tool calling.
ToolContext (Spring AI)
Data passed to tools without exposing it to the model. See Spring AI tools.
Vector database
A store optimised for nearest-neighbour search over embeddings with filters. See Vector databases.
